utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If just before calling the next witness we could tender the exhibits from Witness 167.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We had them on our list, numbers provisionally assigned to them by the registrar. Are there any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, on behalf of the Gotovina Defence, Mr. Misetic had a personal matter to attend to, I'm not sure if he was aware these were going to be tendered right now. I would just ask -- give him the opportunity -- we can tender them and give him the opportunity just to review them and see if he had any further objections. I simply don't know if he does or he doesn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's rather than dealing with part of the list now, leaving out one or two, let's focus on the list soon and not at this moment deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I will communicate with Mr. Misetic and we can reach agreement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then I do understand that there might be quite some time next week to deal with these kind --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- these kind of matters. So that we now would prefer to continue hearing evidence of witnesses. You're ready to call your next witness. No protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Russo will be calling the next witness, so I will step aside, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Russo, your next witness would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution calls Witness 154, Colonel Robert Williams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher is already on her way to accompany the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Williams. Before you give evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. May I invite to you make that solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Williams. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, I see that you appear in uniform in court. I have the habit of addressing military and non-military people all by just saying Mr. Williams. That has got nothing to do with disrespect for your position and your rank but just to inform you, not everyone has the same habit in this courtroom, but I just explain to you why I call you Mr. Williams.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo. Mr. Russo is counsel for the Prosecution and he will be the first one to examine you. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel Williams. If you would please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. My name is Robert Schuman Williams.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Colonel, do you recall giving three statements to the ICTY dated 5 November 1995; 22 August 1996; and 14 November 2007?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I do, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to review those statements before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And in the course of reviewing those statements, did you make a number of corrections and clarifications to them and to their attachments?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I did, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And were those clarifications that you made and corrections reduced in writing in a supplemental information sheet which you reviewed and signed.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please have 65 ter 5484.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Looking at your screen, Colonel Williams, is this the supplemental information sheet which contains the corrections and clarifications to your earlier three statements?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, for the Court's information we have not yet uploaded the B/C/S translation for this document. However, that will be done today.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel Williams, taken together with the corrections and clarifications outlined in this document, are all of your statements true and accurate to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge they are true and accurate, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if you were examined on the same matters in those statements and on this supplemental information sheet, would your answers today be the same?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: They would, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, on that basis I would move for the admission of the three statements and the supplemental information sheet pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm not sure there was any notification about the supplemental information sheet being offered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I sent an e-mail on Tuesday to Defence counsel and also forwarding to Chambers informing them that we did intend to offer this as an expedient in the 92 ter process. I didn't hear any objection. I wasn't sure that there was a misunderstanding about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There clearly was because of -- obviously that that had not been the practice previously. I know that you sent us the supplemental information sheet. That being said, Judge, just reviewing this, I mean, I withdraw any objection. I just was -- for future reference, I would like a little bit more clarity if that is, in fact, what we are doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes they are disclosed just for the purposes of information and sometimes apparently they're disclosed and -- then I take it that apart from seeking them to be admitted, you also ask permission to add them to your 65 ter list, Mr. Russo, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. My apologies for not being specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clear that the Defence, for the future, would like to know whether the supplemental information sheet will be exhibited or whether it is just sent for information. Any other objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The only question I have is the 65 ter on the transcript has one extra number; I just wanted to make sure that we have the correct number.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was going to give the 65 ter numbers for all of the statements including the supplemental information sheet for the registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What you didn't do and what we usually do, Mr. Russo, is to give copies or show them on the screen so that we know for sure that the statements that were -- are admitted and to which the witness gave his attestation that that's the same document as we have in front of us. It has not been done. Now it is usually a formality. If the parties could agree that the witness attested to the statements as standard under the 92 ter --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We so attest. We have no objection. I understand this is a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that we'll pay some attention to the statements anyhow. So if there would be a problem, it would become clear anyhow. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me provide Mr. Registrar with the 65 ter number for --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour. I'm sorry, Mr. Russo, to interrupt. I just have a question regarding, for example, the first statement dated ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: 5 November 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Would the statement include the attachment, would the attachment be a separate exhibit or would that be part of the statement? I just -- just so we're clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: The statement will be submitted without the attachment. The attachment has already come in, as you know, through a prior witness, so we submit in the 92 ter only the statement itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we find the 65 ter numbers already in the -- in the supplemental information sheet, Mr. Russo. First statement, the 1995 statement, 65 ter 5446. Mr. Registrar, that would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P924.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P924 is admitted into evidence. The second statement, 1996 statement, 65 ter 5447 would be, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number P925.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P925 is admitted into evidence. The third statement, the 2007 statement, 65 ter 5448, that would be, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P926, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P926 is admitted into evidence. And then finally we have the supplemental information sheet statement, dated the 23rd of September, 2008, and that would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P927, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P927 is admitted into evidence. And I think the 65 ter number was mentioned earlier by you today, Mr. Russo. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could be allowed to provide the witness with hard copies of his statements at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And with the Chamber's permission, I would like to read a brief summary of the 92 ter statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have explained to the witness that this is to inform the public about the content of the statements we received in written form.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel Robert Williams was a Military Information Officer for the Canadian contingent of the UNPROFOR mission based in Zagreb. On 3 August 1995, he travelled to Knin to gather on-site intelligence regarding the warring factions in Sector South and to brief the Sector South commander regarding the likelihood of a Croatian offensive to retake the Krajina. He noted the lack of defensive positions, as well as the lack of heavy weapons, artillery and tanks in Knin and concluded that the ARSK had no plans to defend the town. He was present in Knin during the artillery attacks on 4 and 5 August, 1995, and observed the shelling of Knin from the balcony of the UN HQ building. He saw no outgoing artillery fire from Knin on either day. Colonel Williams observed that the downtown area of Knin, and the Tvik factory in particular, were heavily hit during the initial salvo which was followed by a period of corrected fire and then what he termed "harassment fire." During the late night on 4 August, Colonel Williams assisted in bringing in and taking care of the Serb refugees who came to the UN HQ compound since he could speak Serbo-Croat. On the morning of 5 August, he was one of the UN officers who went outside the UN compound to remove bodies of several civilians and ARSK soldiers who were killed by a mortar blast at the intersection just outside of the compound. He and other UN officers came under mortar fire at that time. After the HV entered Knin on the afternoon of 5 August, Colonel Williams witnessed HV soldiers drinking and looting outside the UN HQ compound and heard explosions and fires occurring in Knin. That concludes my summary, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel Williams, I'd like to begin with your assessment of the situation in Knin immediately prior to Operation Storm, specifically if you can refer to your second statement, which for the record is P925, at page 3 of that statement, bottom of the second paragraph; and in the B/C/S this appears at page 5 in the first paragraph. Now, that portion of your statement, Mr. Williams, you state: "I remember thinking that it was very strange that the only military heavy equipment was so far away from Knin and that it was no dug-in defensive positions, no artillery, no tanks, no preparation to defend Knin. And my conclusion on the 3 August 1995 was that the RSK have no plans to defend Knin as a town." Colonel, can you tell the Court whether these observations and assessments you made were based on personal observations of yours in the town of Knin on 3 August 1995?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, they were based upon personal observations of the afternoon and evening of the 3rd of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you explain to the Court why you were in Knin on the 3rd of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was in Knin on the 3rd of August, 1995, to brief General Forand, the Canadian commander of Sector South, as far as the possibility or potential of an invasion or of an assault against the Krajina and to explain to him our assessment of the situation in both UN sectors North and South.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And in addition to the observations that you made in the town itself, did you receive any information from any other source regarding the military situation in Knin on the 3rd of August?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I talked to people that had already been in Knin far longer. I noted a lack of activity in the city and certainly a lack of military activity in the city itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving to page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And for the Registrar's benefit, all of the statement references I will be making are to the second statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Moving to page 4, Colonel Williams, middle of the 2nd paragraph, which in the B/C/S appears at page 6 in the first paragraph, you state: "I believe that the HV could monitor everything that happened in the time from the 3 August 1995 in Knin town itself until they took it over 5 August 1995." I'd like you, if you could, please, to explain to the Court why you think the HV could monitor everything that happened in Knin from 3 August onward.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. When I talk about monitor everything, it would be both visual and potentially electronically. And I would say that the accuracy of the artillery fire and the fact that they were able to bring down artillery fire indicates to me they had a good -- the HV, that is, had a good idea of activity in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move now to some of your observations of the artillery attack itself and we'll begin with your observations on 4 August. Referring to page 4, the bottom of the final paragraph, in B/C/S this appears on page 6 in the second paragraph. Where you describe some of the shelling during that day as: "Some type of harassment fire with single or groups of two to three guns shelling different areas of the town, including residential areas. I remember think that the pattern of shelling was to induce the speed of civilian population to leave town." Colonel, can you explain to the Court what you mean by "harassment fire" in the residential areas?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Certainly. What I mean by "harassment fire" is not directed at a specific military targets but one or two shells directed in an area to convince people to leave, not necessarily targeted at a house but near enough to a house or building to encourage the occupants, if they remained, that they should leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And what was it about what you saw that made you think it was intended to speed up the flight of civilians?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The fact that it was fairly sporadic. The heavy bombardment had already occurred earlier in the day. It lessened in the afternoon and then random or fairly random shots in one or two in different areas to encourage people to leave. It was not an intense bombardment from any -- from my point of view and my opinion only, military usefulness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court how long this type of harassment fire continued for during the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This type of harassment fire continued through late afternoon, early into the evening. I could not tell you the exact time I heard the last shot. I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statements you indicate that you had assisted in the intake of the Serb refugees on the 4th of August. Can you tell the Court whether shelling continued during that time-period?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I could not tell the Court for sure whether shelling continued during that time-period. The refugee intake started at 2320 hours, or 11.20 in the evening, on the 4th of August. I was focusing on assisting the refugees not counting artillery shells at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now moving to 5 August and referring to the top of page 6. In B/C/S this is page 8 at the second paragraph. You describe shelling in the early hours of 5 August as follows: "Heavy shelling continued all over the town and several shells impacted close to the HQ. I assessed the impacts close to the HQ being a combination of short fuses and harassment fire against the UN to keep us in the camp." First, when you say that shelling, heavy shelling continued all over the town, can you tell the Court whether this was corrected fire or something different?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. The heavy fire started early in the morning of the 5th, approximately 5.20. Our assessment was it was would probably start at 5.00. By that time, the petroleum storage, the oils in storage by the train station was on fire so some of the effect of the shelling was actually obscured by the black smoke, but it was heavy and in different parts of the town for the first part of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Colonel, why did you assess that some of the rounds landing close to the HQ were meant to harass the UN?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The rounds that landed close to the HQ, and in several cases mud splattered on the balcony, was -- it was an UN camp identified as such, there was no military purpose and there were no Krajina Serb military near the camp. And some of the shells landed several hundred yards due north of the camp, very short of the city. My assessment of the firing on the 4th of August was they had a fairly accurate idea of where they were shelling, so either it was faulty shells or they were fused to land [Realtime transcript read in error "refused to land"] short.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now following on in that same paragraph of your second statement, Colonel, you indicate that at 6.10 a.m. on the 5th of August you saw eight ARSK tanks, one APC and one truck pass the HQ at high speed through Knin and you state: "They never stopped in Knin since I could see and hear them disappear towards the north."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, can you tell the Court whether you saw any attempts being made to target or hit these tanks with artillery?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I saw no attempt made to target or hit these tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Are you able to tell the Court approximately how fast these vehicles were moving?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I would estimate that the vehicles were moving anywhere between 30 and 50 kilometres an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Colonel, did it appear to you that these vehicles were preparing to stand and defend the town?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: At the speed they were moving and until they left my point of view, where I could actually see them, it didn't appear they were slowing down. Once they disappeared from my sight, I can't say what they did after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, Colonel, was there any evidence of damaged or destroyed ARSK vehicles in Knin immediately after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, there was no evidence of destroyed or damaged vehicles in the town from what I saw in the immediate aftermath of Op Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to refer to an aerial photograph of Knin which -- upon which you have marked some areas where you saw shells landing on 4 and 5 August.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please have 65 ter 5485.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps meanwhile I can seek clarification with you, Mr. Williams. What did you exactly mean when you said it -- a combination of short fuses and harassment fire. Harassment fire is quite clear to me. What do you exactly mean by short fuses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The short fuse may have been meant to explode in the air. I noticed in the statement I said -- it says: "They refused to land." I said they were fused to land short, so when you set the fuse on the artillery shell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it is ... it is the way in which they were programmed, more or less, where to explode.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel Williams, taking a look at this aerial photograph, can you explain to the Court what the areas circled in blue represent.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Russo. The areas circled in blue which I circled on this overhead image are the -- the shelling that occurred on the first day, on August 4th, that I could see from the balcony of the headquarters building. Approximate areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell the Court what the areas circled in red signify.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The areas circled in red depict, to the best of my recollection, the corrected fire on particular areas where the -- the initial fire was in the blue, more intense fire later in the day upon the red.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally, the areas which are circled and also shaded in green, can you please explain to the Court what those represent.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Certainly. The areas circled and shaded in green represent shelling on the 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to move this into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number P928.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P928 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel Williams, in your second statement at page 6, the second paragraph, in B/C/S this appears at page 8 in the third paragraph, you describe an incident there on the morning of the 5th of August where you assisted in bagging the bodies of several people who had been killed by a mortar blast at the intersection outside the compound. I would like you, please, in your own words, to describe that incident for the Court.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Certainly. The word had come back to the headquarters through one of my colleagues, Mr. Berikoff and Sergeant Engelby, another colleague, that there had been some wounded or dead people at the intersection, and in order to clear them off the road or move them out of the way to allow any traffic plus the fact that it was -- very warm and the -- the smell of the dead and the traumatic effect upon the approximately 500 refugees we had in camp at the time, or, rather, the Krajina Serb civilians, we wanted to move these people off the road and do any dignity to their remains. So we left the camp. We had a -- a photographer, civilian photographer went with us but did not stay. She immediately became ill upon arriving at the scene, and at the scene, to the best of my recollection, and I can visualize it in my mind still, we found six dead men; one them had looked like he had been killed quite a while ago, if not a day before. The blood was quite crimson on him. He was in a horse-drawn carriage. There was a hunting rifle was near him. His wife or sister was nearby saying the Lord's Prayer over him in Serbian, [B/C/S spoken]. She was crying her son or nephew was dead next to the cart. Neither of those two gentlemen had uniforms on. The other four individuals, one was a Mr. Djapic. I -- when we were crawling on the ground I wanted to verify as best we could who these people were so that in the event that the remains disappear, as can happen in the carnage of war, we could at least identify the Red Cross or Red Crescent so they could notify the next of kin and they could have closure for their families. The other three individuals, two were in the uniform of Krajina Serb, no rank, no insignia and no identification in any of the other five. So the only person we could identify was Mr. Djapic from Drnis, according to his papers. While we were picking up their remains, a mortar shell went off between 15 and 20 feet in the air above us at the time. Even though it was hot and even though we didn't want to, we wore our blue helmets for protection which made us stand out, and once we got the individuals into what we call body-bags or plastic bags with zippers to take them off the road, we left. Before we did that, I tried to encourage -- whether she was the wife or sister of the elderly gentleman killed to come with us. She was severely wounded. Her -- her right eye was hanging out. She was bleeding. And fortunately, two days later I did see her in the camp. I'm not sure how she got in but she eventually came in. That is my best recollection of the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Colonel Williams. In your statement you reference an UN CIVPOL report regarding this incident and I'd like to ask you a few questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please have Exhibit P220.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel Williams, taking a look at your screen, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I do, sir, and I recognise my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Is this the UNCIVPOL report which you mention in your second statement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It appears to be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now the report indicates, in the last paragraph there, that as of 6 August 1995 at 1315 hours, the body of one of the ARSK soldiers had been moved whereas the rest remained in the same place. Are you able to clarify for the Court whether this was the same body which you later indicate you saw mutilated on the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This was the same body we saw mutilated and I saw mutilated on the corner on the 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And the last male listed in the report is the one who appears to have suffered a gunshot wound to the chest. Do you have any information for the Court about how or when that gunshot happened?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have no information as to how or where that gunshot wound happened. I had asked his -- either his wife or sister what had happened but she was in a state of shock and unable to explain what had happened to that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I believe you've already touched on this, the report does mention strong evidence that this man was father and possibly father of the other young man who was killed. Can you tell Court what this evidence was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The evidence -- the young man and the elderly gentleman, the young man was hanging off the cart and the woman with was them and she would not leave them. So that was my inference that they were related. She would not leave the two people. The elderly gentleman was laying in the cart and so they had taken his dead body with them. So to me it indicated that they were somehow related, though I can't say with 100 percent certainty that they were related.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, before we move on to discuss some of the events following the artillery attack, can you tell the Court whether during the attack itself you continued in your duties as an intelligence officer and made reports on the situation to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: During the course of the day, I would brief our commander, General Forand, and other staff, Colonel Leslie included. I attempted and was successful upon more than one occasion to communicate to the Canadian contingent headquarters in Zagreb to explain to them the situation and actually at one point managed to get a phone call through to the Canadian National Defence headquarters in Ottawa to explain that the war had started and that we were in, what I would call, only awkward situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And what were these reports that you made based on?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Reports were based on personal observation reports coming in from the Czech battalion that was in our sector, a fellow Canadian Battalion that was in the sector and then at one point debriefing a Czech soldier who had arrived and various reporting, random and somewhat sporadic, from our Kenyan Battalion colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And in these reports you made, did you consider any media information?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir. We had information provided by a media person. His first name is Alun, I can picture him but I don't recall his last name. I generally recall it was A-l-u-n, which I had never seen as a spelling for Alun. And there was reporting we -- included in there and indicated it was, for the most part, media reporting, though I'm not sure all of it was cited as media reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please have 65 ter 1927.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Looking at your screen, Colonel Williams, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And is this one of the documents upon which you relied in making your intelligence assessments on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct. In particular the paragraph where the losses to the Croatian soldiers killed in the offensive of 200. We had no proof of that other than the reporting which, as I mentioned, we had no way of confirming at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. The information which follows that indicates that in listening to Croatian army communications some HV commander was supposedly heard to indicate that his soldiers were deserting the front line. Was this information something which you considered accurate and why or why not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I didn't consider this information accurate because my assessment and the assessment of my intelligence colleagues was the Croatian army was professional and extremely well trained and it's not something they would do. We read this as likely propaganda by the Krajina Serbs to try to bolster their own morale or to try to weaken the morale of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour. With all due respect, Colonel, that is speculation, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are not objecting against the question but against the answer, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Frankly, Judge, they're part and parcel of each other. To the extent that he can report what was reported in the radio, I -- that's fine. But his speculation on that score is something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If I could, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Previous witnesses, in particular Mr. Dangerfield and Mr. Berikoff, there was, I believe, the radio broadcast by General Mrksic or the broadcast of his interview and they were -- the Defence put those statements to the witnesses and were asked for their opinions about whether they agreed with those statements or not. I don't believe this is any different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, if I may. I certainly put General Mrksic's public radio broadcast to the witness. I didn't put whether or not, for instance, Mr. Berikoff agreed with what General Mrksic had to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do believe the follow-up questions were, if the Court recalls, based on the truthfulness or asking the witness to assume that, for example, units were withdrawing for the defence of Knin was in fact true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- let's -- one second. Let me give a second to think about the matter and re-read the question and ... The witness may answer the question in respect of whether he formed an opinion at the time when you learned about this broadcast, whether you formed an opinion about the accuracy and on what that assessment -- on what that opinion was based. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My opinion at the time would be 200 is a very exact figure and it is hard to estimate exact figures in a time of war and that the Croatian army would be unlikely to take that loss on the first day. They were very well trained and organised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your opinion was based on what you knew about the professionality of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. At this time I would move for the admission of 65 ter 1927.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number P929.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P929 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel Williams, moving now to the events following the artillery attack, let me refer you to page 6 of your second statement at the third paragraph. And in B/C/S this appears at page 9 in the first paragraph. And there you indicate that at 1205 hours the 7 Guards Brigade showed up at the gate of the UN compound. First, I'd like to you please explain to the Court how you know what unit of the HV they were from?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Russo. The 7 Guards Brigade from Varazdin, their emblem was a Puma and they wore that as a patch and it was on many of their vehicles, on the side of the hull of the turret of the tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did you speak to any of these HV soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And did you speak to them in Croatian or in English?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I spoke to the first gentleman in Croatian. I wished him good day, explained who we were. His first question to me and his only question was where was Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did you tell him where Martic was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: When I told him I had no idea where Martic was, he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Who did you speak to after that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The second soldier, a soldier came up to me, not an officer and said to me in perfect Canadian English, What the hell are you guys doing here?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: How did you respond to that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I said, We are part of the United Nations headquarters in Sector South and there's a number of Canadians here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel, are you able to tell the Court whether there were any senior HV officers present when the HV arrived at the gate?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The first presence at the gate was three tanks. Until this gentleman walked over, the three tanks sat there for several minutes. So I'm not sure if he came from one of the tanks. I doubt it because he was not in a uniform that they were wearing. He was in more of a clean uniform and appeared to walk over to the gate, alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And was this gentleman a senior officer?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This gentleman was at least a lieutenant-colonel in the Croatian army, in the HV.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Staying in that same paragraph, Colonel, you state: "I remember that I was thinking that the HV wanted to make sure that we, the UN, stayed put in the camp so that follow-up HV units and so-called Croatian special police could continue into town and conduct their activities unobserved." First, what made you believe that Croatian special police were involved?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I had no evidence that the Croatian special police were involved but the Croatian police would follow-up the initial fighting forces as happened in Op Flash and seemed to be the tactic of the Croatian military. The second individual I spoke to, the Canadian or Canadian citizen, if I guess, but I'm not sure if he still was, indicated that we should stay in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And what was it that made you think that they didn't want the UN to observe what they were doing in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The -- we were on the south part of the city and they still had to capture the entire city; so whether they wanted us out of the way or not observe would be speculation on my behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel, are you able to tell the Court whether at any time after these Croatian soldiers arrived at the gate you saw or heard any shells landing in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There were a limited number of shells landing in Knin after the soldiers arrived at the gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you give the Court an idea of approximately how many and when?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon, the exact number I couldn't specify. There was not as many as the day before, the 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, moving to the top of the next page, which, in B/C/S is page 9, second paragraph, you mention drinking and looting by HV soldiers that you witnessed from the balcony of the UN HQ building and I would like to you, please, describe what you saw exactly to the Court.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: All right. Looking out from the balcony, down on to the street directly in front of the UN camp, I observed soldiers with rifle in one hand and various -- with either television in the other hand, one of them walking with a television on top of his shoulder holding it. Some with radios, and different household articles that one would -- I would not expect to see with a combat force.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you give the Court any idea of whether any HV officers or commanders were present when this behaviour was ongoing?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I did not see any rank that would indicate an officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Was this drinking and looting occurring in a manner which was open or concealed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There was drinking occurring in the lot just across the road from the headquarters and it was what I would call somewhat civilized. There was people having a drink, they were probably tired.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Would it have been apparent to anyone on the scene what was happening?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The fact of soldiers walking with televisions and items they would not have brought into combat, to me, was definitely out of the ordinarily. Somebody understanding what an assault force would do would have a good idea that that was unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And moving to the third paragraph of that page, you mention an incident which occurred at 1900 hours on the evening of 5 August where you and other UN members attempted to get into Knin town itself and I'd like you to please describe for the Court what happened then.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Right. We had made an attempt using Canadian armoured personnel carrier, and our Czech colleagues with their armoured personnel carriers, and we were blocked at the intersection by a column of T-55 tanks from 7 Brigade, the Puma. They indicated to us they had right of way. Their vehicles were larger and they indicated by waving that they wanted us off the road, so we returned to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And on the way back to the camp, Colonel, did you see any dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I saw one dead body. I saw the same body when I left the camp. It's of a young soldier that attempted to surrender to us earlier in the day, a Krajina Serb soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you give the Court some information about this soldier that you saw earlier in the day?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Earlier in the day he attempted to surrender to myself and one of my colleagues at the front gate. I explained that we could not take his surrender because we did not want to endanger the life of the civilians by harbouring potential military or military soldiers in the Krajina army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And are you certain this is the same individual whom you saw dead outside of the compound later on that evening?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have no doubt it is the same individual. I can picture his face perfectly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, if you know, how he appeared to have died?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He was laying in a ditch. His head was to the side and he a gunshot in the back of his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. In the next paragraph, you mention a trip into town to meet with the Special Representative Akashi on the 7th of August, and you state: "At this time the Croats had worked hard to clean up everything." Can you please describe for the Court what you know about this clean-up effort?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The only thing I can describe about any clean up effort was when we had left the intersection on the -- when picking up the six bodies. There was quite a bit of carnage, destruction of the road, blood from the dead, body parts, and when we drove out on the 7th, there was nothing. The road was absolutely clean. It looked like nothing had ever happened there. That's the only first eye-witness account I can give you. I'm not aware of any other.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And also in that paragraph it indicates: "Looting were going on all over the town. This was the 7 Puma Brigade, 4 Guards Brigade, elements from the 3 Guards Brigade, approximately a company, however, with no vehicles, 66 and 72nd MP units and some Home Guard units." First, Colonel, can you clarify what day you are referring to this looting occurring?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The 6th of August. This is from reporting that I had. This is not from firsthand observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court what the identification of the units where that information came from?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The 7th Brigade, by the brigade insignia; the 4th Guards Brigade, by the brigade insignia; the 3rd Guards, by the colour of berets that were observed; and the 66th and 72nd MP units. The 72nd are identified and the 66th was assessed, so not definite.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court how you identified Home Guard units?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Home Guard units were usually in a slightly different uniform and they had a patch, some had two patches, representing -- one was representing the actual regiment of what Home Guard regiment it was; and the other ones had a patch they wore on their sleeve which would have [B/C/S spoken], or Home Defence, on the patch.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you describe for the Court the appearance of these Home Guard units as compared to those of the 7, 4, or 3 Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The Home Guard units appeared to be what I can only say is scruffy and I don't mean that in a derogatory sense. They seemed to be not as well fed or not as -- physically as big or as physically fit as the Guards units. Some had hats, some did not; some were shaven, some were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, when did you leave Knin?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I left Knin on the 7th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And how exactly did you leave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I flew out on a Sea King helicopter which was evacuating one of our wounded to hospital and I flew to Split by helicopter and then from Split to Zagreb by an UN aircraft, a Yak 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Colonel --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel, can you tell the Court what, if anything, you observed on the helicopter flight out of Knin itself.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I observed at various time in the flight, particularly near Knin, buildings on fire, houses, and in some cases livestock dead in the field, as in livestock were not moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you give the Court some idea of the scale of this kind of destruction?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The only thing I can say with certainty about the scale is it wasn't just a random house. There were many houses, certainly more than one and more than one field of dead livestock.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, you've made several reports regarding the events surrounding Operation Storm, one of which has already been admitted into evidence. I would like, however, to confirm another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If, Mr. Registrar, we could, please, have 65 ter 3989.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Looking at your screen, Colonel, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court whether or not you authored this document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I compiled this document from a variety of sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you give the Court an idea of what those sources were?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Certainly Mr. Russo. The sources I used were UN reporting from different battalions. Eye-witness accounts, things I observed, things that some of my colleagues observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Colonel, what was the purpose of creating this particular document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The purpose of my creating this document was to try to understand why Knin had fallen so quickly and to determine in -- a military point of view, what is it we missed in the assessment of the potential foreign assault on the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you give the Court a time-frame for when this document was created?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I created this document after I had returned to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would move for the admission of 65 ter 3989.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number P930.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P930 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel Williams, at any time after Operation Storm did you ever hear a mention of or any indication of the existence of warlords in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No. And that's not a term that I have ever heard used nor would I have used to describe any of the military commanders in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Just so we're clear, what is your understanding of that term, warlords?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: My understanding of warlord would be an uncontrolled militia hired by some criminal is the context we've used it in other theatres of operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, did any Croatian official ever mention the existence of warlords as having been responsible for any of the conduct in Sector South, following Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have never, ever heard any mention of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, that conclude my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Russo. Mr. Kehoe, you will be the first one to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, I will. If I could just have one moment to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, to get the right furniture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, you will be cross-examined first by Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kehoe is counsel for Mr. Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very good, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel Williams. Good to see you again, sir.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, good to see you again as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, I would like to talk to you a bit about some of the reporting that you did and the first one, just preliminarily, was the document that you were just discussed with Mr. Russo, which was your 1996 statement, P925. Now, Colonel, you had, prior to going to Knin in August, been monitoring the activities of the HV coming up the Livno valley and into the Dinara, had you not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, we had, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And even prior to coming to Knin, you knew that there was a build-up not only in Sector South -- excuse me, let me say that again there was a build-up by the HV not only in Sector South but also in Sector North?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say that before you got to Knin to brief General Forand, you expected the HV to engage in a large, concerted operation against the Krajina Serbs throughout Sector North and Sector South. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is accurate, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, I understand from your report that you came to Zagreb, I believe, in June of 1995. And if I can turn our attention to your chronology that has come into evidence under another witness, which is P744. That's the document that sets forth the situation from 8 July to 18 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can put that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, I noticed here, sir, that you have in the insert for July the 23rd, HV shelling in the Cetina valley. Do you see that, July the 23rd?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And then we go back down to the 26th. Again we have 18 artillery shells impacted in the general area of Cetina village and the slope of Antica Glava heights. Now, if I can, and just if I can just orient us with the map and if I can go to D728, page 6 of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher [sic]. I'm sorry, D728, page 6 of D728.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if I may, Colonel as an intelligence officer, you were made aware, of course, about the movements by the HV in the Livno and up in the Dinara even before you came to Zagreb towards the latter part of June of 1995. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And let me show you a map. This operation - this is Jump 2. If we can go to the next page of this. This references the combat operations in Operation Jump 2 between 4 June and 11 June 1995. And if I could just focus, if I could just blow-up the centre of that just a little bit near the 1st Light Infantry Brigade. There we go. Now, the 1st Light Infantry Brigade that you see there for the ARSK was located in Vrlika, was it not, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have not seen this map before but that seems to be, to my recollection, where we had locate the them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this is -- reflects the fighting in Jump 2 -- Operation Jump 2 between 4 June and 11 June of 1995, and throughout that time, Colonel, you learned that there was a significant amount of fighting back and forth along this confrontation line, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you a video, if I can, and I want to show you the video, Colonel, I know you haven't seen it before, maybe you have. As part of your intelligence gathering capabilities, were you monitoring the media on both the Croatian side and the RSK side?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I personally was not but we had staff, UN staff that were monitoring both communications, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay, and -- I'm just taking a brief pause for the translators, so if I do that, just bear with me. And naturally if something of interest came to your attention -- came to their attention, they would then tell you as part of the G2 section or the Intel section, correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me -- if I can just take one moment and get this D number correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is -- Mr. Usher, this is 1D55-0007. This is a video-clip from Dnevnik News, 6 June 1995. And, Your Honour, the translations have been given to the translation booths.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] After the latest aggression directed at Srpska and Krajina, the president of the RSK, Milan Martic, visited the soldiers and the local inhabitants of Podinarje today." "Tatjana Batak: With respect to the latest aggression, Milan Martic visited the village of Cetina at the base of this mountain where the shelling began two days ago and spoke to the soldiers in the villages of Cetina." "Milan Martic: The situation on the battlefront has stabilized and I can say that I'm pleased. I expect the situation to be even better. The confidence among men has been restored and the call up for mobilisation" in the field was successful. Additional forces are arriving from nearly every region of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, Republika Srpska and even Serbia to the jeopardized locations, including this area as well. "I expect that the situation will change significantly in the following period. We have increased our measures in a military sense. "The initial period from the attack on Western Slavonia and the shattered confidence in certain parts of the Krajina has been restored and it's a whole different story now. Many countries in the world are slowly changing their media propaganda and their diplomatic delegates in the Security Council and in other places are taking a sharper approach towards Croatia and we shall emerge as the winners of this battle, I believe."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now Colonel, going to the information in this -- had you seen this before?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I had not seen this video before, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You told us you were aware of this -- this fighting or had Intel on this fighting, and do you know what steps the ARSK took in June of 1995 to, as Milan Martic says, stabilize the situation on the battle front?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of what steps he took in June 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, of the defences put forth by the ARSK in June of 1995 while Operation Jump 2 was ongoing?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the defences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Lastly on this score, there is a quote -- and -- that would playing it back Colonel, Martic says: "Additional forces are arriving from every region of the RSK, the RS, Republika Srpska, and even in Serbia to the jeopardized locations." Did the Intel reporting reflect at that time that these additional resources were coming to the battle front area near Cetina from every region of the RSK, the Republika Srpska or even Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any Intel reporting that. My focus was on the -- Croatia and the Krajinas, not Bosnia itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, the Cetina valley is in the Krajina, sir.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I realize that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we will offer into evidence 1D55-0007.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if I may -- I am sorry. I'm sorry, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D811.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D811 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My apologies for getting in front of the Court, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may just turn our attention back to P744 to the insert for the 26th of July. Now, Colonel, this is the insert of 18 shells impacted in the general area of Cetina and the slopes of Antica Glava. Now -- I say between 10.00 and 1600 on the 26th. Now let me bring up for you at this point 1D55-0018. As this is coming up, if I can just ask you some preliminary questions. As part of your intelligence gathering function, did you on occasion obtain documents from either the HV side or the ARSK side that were of interest to you to allow you to make certain assessments as to what was going on?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I really understand your question. Are you referring to maps or reports or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Maps, or if someone came across an order, or someone came across some type of plans. Did you ever have that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If documents were found, they would be turned into us but none were actually given to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you this then. This is a report of the 25th of July, 1995, a day before your insert in your report. And it is a report from the Operative Group North and it notes: Mr. Commander, during the day -- and this is from the HV, by the way, HV Main Staff, Colonel Ante Kotromanovic [phoen]. This commander or HV commander says: During the day, the enemy engaged in combat activities in the AOR of operative group Sinj as follows. Around 14 hours with seven projectiles from Suhopolje onto Antica Glava . This is for the 25th. Now Antica Glava, by the 25th of July, was a position that was being held by the HV, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, the information that you have in your report reflects -- on the 26th of July, reflects impacts on the slopes of Antica Glava?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you at that point when you -- this information was coming in to you, did you know that that was a position that was being held by the HV on the 25th and the 26th of July?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I did not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The next line, sir: "Around 1800 hours with twelve 120-millimetre mortars from Preocani (Cetina)."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm seeing the letter on the Operational Group North. I'm not seeing the summary of what I provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No. What I'm saying, sir, is I'm just staying with this document, but I was referring back to your report, 744.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, if I may, does he have a hard copy of 744, because I know that was part of his initial statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, he does. It's in the back of the tabs provided to him. It's the last tab.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The first page of that document. I'm talking about the 26th July insert.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: All right. I have it now, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's quite all right. Colonel, if there's any point that you need to reference back to a document, please stop me to allow you to give you the time to do so. Now just looking at your document, this -- the information that you put down in your report of 26th July, that was information that you received from the field. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You weren't there yourself?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if we turn back to the document that's on the screen, this report of the 25th of July, 1995, I note in your report that the shooting that was taking place both at 1400 hours from Suhopolje on to Antica Glava as well as at 1800 hours the mortars coming from Preocani, those two inserts are not in your report. Now, does that mean that that shooting didn't happen, sir, or it means it wasn't reported?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I believe Mr. Kehoe asked the witness whether or not his intelligence information was based on documents received. He indicated he received no documents and now it is being put to him that information in this document wasn't included in his intelligence report. I'm not sure if -- I'm not sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... apparently Mr. Kehoe is it seeking whether what he finds in certain documents, whether that's reflected in the reports prepared by this witness. It's not part of the question that he may have left it out although he would have received that. That's not the question. Mr. Kehoe is just seeking, I take it, to establish how accurate or not the reports were and in his questioning he includes information which may not have been available to the witness. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, did you understand my question, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I understood your question, Mr. Kehoe. I have not seen the report nor would I edit out parts of it if I had seen the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I -- my next question based on that, Colonel, is this: Looking at the report that is on the screen, and of course understanding that it's not in your report, does that mean it didn't happen, the shooting that is reported in July 25th, or just that it wasn't reported back to you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The fact that I'm not aware of it obviously, Mr. Kehoe, doesn't mean it didn't happen. If it happened or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Looking at this particular document in conjunction with the insert that you have in P744 for the 26th of July, you would agree with me, Colonel, that what this reflects is shooting back and forth across the confrontation line, the HV on to the ARSK and the ARSK on to the HV?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, if the information in this report is accurate, then I would agree with you. But I have no way of knowing whether it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I'll offer into evidence 1D55-0018.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D812.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D812 is admitted into evidence. Let me just try to understand fully your question and also the answer, Mr. Kehoe. One report is what happened on the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document is about what happened on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 25th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say shooting both directions would include shooting in one direction one day and then shooting back the next day. Is that how I have to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may clear this up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us just go from your document, sir, for the 26th of July. If the general area of Cetina is a position being held by the ARSK where impacts are reported, and the area of Antica Glava heights is a position that's being held by the HV, you are reporting impacts in the both of those locations. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And would that not indicate to you, based on the impacts in those locations, that the ARSK is firing on the HV and the HV is firing on the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If I had reporting to indicate that firing had occurred from both sides, I would have included that. As I mentioned, the document you provided, it is the first time I'm seeing that. If that is accurate, and I have no reason to say it is or isn't, then I would agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't know if that tends to lend a bit of clarity to the issue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It certainly reduces the time issue to six hours rather than to two days. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On that score, the entry that you have is for the 26th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the particular order that's on the screen, Judge, is it's from a day prior to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm aware of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The submission, Your Honour, I didn't want the -- to lead the Court to believe that we are submitting this as happening on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, going back, if we may, to your reconnaissance, without rehashing, you viewed the build-up in Sector North and then on your helicopter ride down on the 3rd, I do believe it was on the 3rd, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On the 3rd you viewed the HV building up yet again. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you got to Knin, the individual who assisted you and drove you around was Captain Berikoff, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, basically, sir, as you were driving around, it was Captain Berikoff who informed you of the various facilities around Knin that you were driving past. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: In the downtown, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you know that he just got to the area on the 21st of July.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And Captain Berikoff noted for this Court, page 7702, he noted that: "Prior to the offensive, my task was to go to various areas of Sector South, and Knin was not one of my priority tasks in this area. I knew the military facilities on the main street and the main area. Those that were off the main streets, I was not aware of." So you would agree with me, sir, that as you were driving through Knin, Captain Berikoff's knowledge as to the various facilities and their various uses in Knin was limited?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. First, I should have risen a bit earlier. The procedure which is being conducted here is, to my mine, a bit opposite to what we had agreed to. If there is something in the witness's statement which is different from what Mr. Berikoff's testimony indicates, I believe Mr. Kehoe should put Mr. Williams's statement to him first and then confront him with what Mr. Berikoff has to say. What is happening now is Mr. Kehoe telling Mr. Williams essentially what Mr. Berikoff about his limited knowledge, and now he's telling Mr. Williams to agree to Mr. Berikoff's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. This is a Prosecution witness who told this Court that his knowledge of facilities in Knin --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can we have the witness please take his earphones off at this discussion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He might understand some of this, Mr. Russo. If the matter is covered by the statement that is in evidence, then there's no need to ask again to the witness what he knows about the event, because then he has already told us what it is about. The guidance of the Chamber is that no evidence given by another witness should be put to a witness who's then -- who is examined. If not, prior to putting it to him, he has given his own answers to questions related to the matter covered by the other evidence. Now, I would have to check exactly ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If I could add to that, Your Honour. Mr. Williams is now being asked about either the basis or the full extent of Mr. Berikoff's knowledge which is not contained in Mr. Williams's statement. So he should first be asked what he knows about the extent or depth of Mr. Berikoff's knowledge before he is confronted with what Mr. Berikoff has to say about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not part of the guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You take the witness to the 21st of July, Mr. Kehoe, and what exactly is it in his statement or is it in this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In his statement on page 7702.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's the testimony of Mr. Berikoff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now -- I'm now asking myself where you have dealt with the matter, Mr. Berikoff, also dealt with in this statement of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This witness has testified that he came --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you guide me to where exactly to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 3 of his second statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That would be of P25. The first full paragraph at the top. "When we went back to Knin where Captain Berikoff took me around the town and we discussed the town and the terrain around Knin, this was a very helpful discussion for me when later on assessing the attack on Knin by the HV." Now that goes to the very heart of what Captain Berikoff knew or didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would completely disagree with that. It says it was a helpful discussion for him. Mr. Williams doesn't indicate anywhere in his statement what he knows about the depth of Mr. Berikoff's knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
