utterances.text: Let's -- perhaps it takes less time perhaps to ask the witness first the question suggested by Mr. Russo and then we can move on and then go into further depth of this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, I don't know if you want to take a break right now and I can ask Mr. Russo what he wants me to ask, because I'm completely at sea on this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I see that there's a slight difference. It is perceived apparently by the two parties in a different way. You've got 25 minutes to see what Mr. Russo would suggest you ask first. We'll have a break for 25 minutes. We resume at ten minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I'm fully confident that you resolved the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We have resolved the matter and I think that we have clarified it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, suffice it to say, that -- and I just refer you back to -- if I may, Mr. Russo does the witness have a copy of his supplemental information sheet?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, he does. That should be at the -- I believe the fourth tab.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Suffice it say, Colonel, that when Captain Berikoff was driving you around on the 3rd of August and explaining various facilities to you, he, in fact, got some wrong, didn't he? And I refer you to your supplemental sheet, the corrections under 65 ter 5547, where you note that Captain Berikoff told that you the Tvik factory was an ARSK weapons storage site. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I see that and that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. And how many other facilities did Captain Berikoff inform you of that he was incorrect about, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Captain Berikoff did not talk specifically about any other facilities. The tour of Knin, that was he and I. I asked him to take me to Strmica so that I could see the check-point there. So I directed that part of the tour. I knew where we were going to. But in Knin, I couldn't specify other ones that he actually talked about. I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And how long was -- I'm sorry. How long was this drive around Knin that you had with Captain Berikoff?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This drive was several hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would that have included your drive into Strmica and back or just in the town of Knin?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Just in the town of Knin itself, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you also told us in your statement that -- and I quote you on your 1996 statement, on page 3, that: "It is difficult for me to make an accurate assessment about the civilian population since I had just arrived in Knin." Do you see that, sir? That's in the first full paragraph on page 3, about five lines down. Do you see it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, I'm still looking for it, sir. Page 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's your 19 -- it's P25, your 1996 statement.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Page 3. First -- not the carry-over paragraph but the first full paragraph about five lines down: "It is difficult."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Right. I see it now, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, in addition to having limited knowledge about the Knin area, you had a very limited -- you had no knowledge about the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. I had no way of telling whether what I saw on the street was the same or average from previous days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Likewise, you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sorry, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The -- yes. The pause is not only for finalising the translation but also to take a breath. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Likewise, sir, you saw, if you go down two further lines: "Soldiers walking around."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you also saw -- if we just go ahead a day, troop transports, ARSK troop transports, moving through Knin on the 4th, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm trying to find that line, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me go back to 744, which is your chronology. And if I can take you to the 5th of August at 1330. And that would be four pages in on P744. Now, if you note that in the insert for 1330, in the middle of page, are you with me, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I am, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You note in the last sentence in that entry that: "The ARSK troop transport vehicles we saw yesterday are now back."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Right, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So from that, sir, that indicates that you saw troop -- ARSK troop transports moving or in Knin on the 4th of August. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That I don't recall, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, I do understand this is some years down the line, but the chronology that you set forth in 744 was done shortly after the events in Knin from the 4th to the 7th or even the latter part of August of 1995, were they not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So based on the record that you kept, you at least indicate that you saw ARSK troop transports on the 4th.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I would agree with that and I have no reason to doubt it but I do not recollect that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Colonel, I appreciate that. I know it's been a long time, sir. I do appreciate that. Let me turn our attention just briefly to the troops and I would like to show you a piece from a book that has been introduced certainly in part to date by General Sekulic, an ARSK operations commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what I'd like to bring up is 1D44-0003. And once it comes up I would like in that, page 0126. In English, I'm sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just for reference purposes, Colonel, this was written by the ARSK General Sekulic, which was the commander or chief of operations. Now, if I can just go down to the bottom portion of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand there is a B/C/S version but it is a little difficult to match up per se. If we could move ahead with just the English at this point, I think we could -- it might be a bit quicker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the -- the B/C/S version is primarily serving the interests of the accused and, of course, the public. So, therefore, I would urge you to at least find it but at the same time we can proceed, if --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. They will be searching for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, this is a comment by General Sekulic and do you see the paragraph: "Prior to the 4th of August."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It notes: "Prior to 4 August, this combat group coordinated with police battalion and the 2nd Guards Brigade in the defence of Dinara. On the day when Oluja," which is Storm, "started, the Guards Brigade was not in Dinara but resting in Knin." Does that refresh your recollection in any fashion, Colonel, of the soldiers that you observed and you talked about in your statement or in these troop transports that you may have observed on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It doesn't, Mr. Kehoe. I didn't see any indication of any unit flashes or any large number of soldiers. So I couldn't identify what unit they were from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, where do we see the troops -- in the troop transport vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If -- Your Honour, what -- what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to -- oh, you say you may have observed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Look at the insert on 744 at -- on the 5th of August at 1330.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It says that the vehicles were --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- yes, but it doesn't say anything about who were in the vehicles, neither the day before nor on that same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore if we -- we should limit ourselves to what the text says especially if the witness has no recollection of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And with all due respect, Judge, what I'm trying to do is -- the witness said he didn't recall the troop movement on the 4th, and I was just trying to show him another document with the hopes of refreshing his recollection if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In that you now put the troops into the troop transport vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... what I was more interested is just if, in fact, that refreshed his recollection as to the troops, if any, that he observed on the 4th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I'll offer into evidence 1D44-0126.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D813.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But just ... let me just -- it is a -- it is part of a book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we limit ourselves to these pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I just want to know for sure. Of course I could check that what exactly the document is, how long it is. Is it a selection of the book?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It has been, Judge. And we have been in a series of discussions and put selections of this book in with the hopes of ultimately putting the entire compilation in. It is -- the excerpts that we have so far uploaded in D44-0003 is pages 156 to 247.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, the issue is simply the following. You are putting a page to the witness and then we have to check -- we have no 65 ter numbers neither do we have -- so then we have to check in the -- I do understand that what you now tender into evidence, but let me check that, is an 81-page document. So we are not tendering at this moment one or two or three pages just for the context but the document uploaded under this number is 88 pages. One page has been used and now, of course, the Chamber wants to avoid -- if we look at one page that we always get, for nothing, another hundred attached to it, where we have no guidance as to the relevance of the other pages, et cetera. So I -- you're invited to -- to select for the purposes of introduction of this piece of evidence through this witness relevant pages sufficient to have context and the -- and the portion we specifically dealt with and not to present as another almost 80 pages in addition to that, which we would not know what to do with it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may by way of clarity, Judge, some of those other pages have been used in various -- in various times during the course of this, and we will be using it in the future as well. I understand the difficulties and I understand that Your Honour and the Bench does not want clutter, for lack of a better of term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have so many books to read, Mr. Kehoe, that we're not seeking other ones but we want to read the relevant evidence which is introduced in an efficient way through a witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then, at this moment, it cannot be admitted as it stands now. Make a further selection. We know Mr. Russo has no objections and if finally, page by page, we get the whole book, then perhaps we could reorganize at the end and say it is one book which is in evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, I'd just like to shift subjects to just move on to the actual shelling of the 4th of August. Now, the first point is that you note in your -- P26, your 2007 statement, that -- in paragraph 2 that the -- "appeared to me that the purpose" -- we're talking about the shelling. "It appeared to me that the purpose was to induce the civilian population to flee." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: You said paragraph 2, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sorry, paragraph 3 in your 2007 statement, that would be P926.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Right. I see that in paragraph 3, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now in your supplemental information sheet, you noted that the reports from UN personnel regarding targeting of purely residential areas came from UN CIVPOL and UN military personnel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you do not know that of your own personal knowledge, because you didn't observe any shelling of civilian areas.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: My observation point was from the balcony of the UN headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. My question is from the -- your observation point, you cannot tell this Chamber that you observed any shelling of civilian areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The -- later on in that same paragraph you can read: "What I mean by that is that purely civilian areas were hit by shells during this time."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, my question -- this is cross-examination and if Mr. Russo wants to resuscitate the witness, he can. But the issue is did he observe the shelling of civilian areas, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, then he should be pointed to the portions of his statement which address where he says he saw that and then to ask him if it is either true or not, not to put it to him in the context of not knowing where he say it in any of his three or four statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, I think the question was whether from the witness' observation point that -- whether he could or could not, it was suggested that he could not tell the Chamber, that he observed any of the shelling and we'll hear the answer of the witness, and whereas you find reasons in his statement to deny that it is correct, we'll hear from the witness. He will tell us. The question whether you could observe the shelling from your observation point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it was suggested that you could not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not observe the impact of shells from my point of view, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the actual counting that you talk about in your supplemental sheet and also in some detail at -- in your 1996 statement at page 4 where you note -- sorry. Starting at the top of page 4 where you talk about where, "We were counting the shells coming in." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The first paragraph or the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The first paragraph, the carry over paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Right, I see that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now the counting of the shells, sir, this is a count that you got in large part from Colonel Leslie. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's not correct, okay. Let me show you P102. Now, this is an UNMO situation report for the 4th of August at 1200. The first full paragraph -- excuse me, this is -- is this -- if we can go to, I'm sorry, P101. My apologies. My apologies, Colonel and to the Court. This is an UNMO report and look at the first paragraph: "HV shelling on Knin started on the 4th at 0500, August, and continued up till the 4th at 1040. Total around 350 to 400 artillery MRL rocket fire were heard by the UNMOs in Knin." Do you agree to that number, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have not seen this report before. I have no reason to doubt that that's what they thought the artillery fire was from the UNMO point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the UNMOs were located in UN Sector South in the same location you were. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: For the most part they were, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you also note in your report that -- this is on, again, your 1996 report in the first carry over paragraph that MRLs, M63s were used?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now were these used by the ARSK or being used by the HV?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: My understanding was that the HV had them in your inventory, not the ARSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: My understanding from previous reporting and from our understanding of what equipment went to what countries when the former Yugoslavia broke up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you D85. As this is coming up, where were the HV positions at that time? Fire -- artillery positions?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. At what time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The morning of the 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The morning of the 4th of August, I and several other individuals were counting shells that were coming over the camp, so from the south of the UN camp in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, would it be fair to say that the firing positions that you observed by the HV were well in excess of ten kilometres away, ten to 20 kilometres away?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The range of the artillery could make that possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us look at the M63. And this is an item that gives the actual range of an M63 as 8.6 kilometres. So if you, in fact, observed M63 shells being fired that day, it couldn't have been by the HV, could it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If I understand your question correctly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, let's first analyse questions and answers we had early. You said -- the witness said that the artillery was fired from the south and came over their heads. He didn't give any distance. Then your next question was, whether it would be fair to say that the firing positions you observed were well in excess of ten kilometres away, ten to 20 kilometres away. You suggested it could have been ten to 20 kilometres. Then the witness said: "The range of the artillery could make that possible." Now what then follows that in your question you start from a point of view that it was at that distance. That's certainly not what was said by the witness. It has not been established in any way. The only thing the witness says that if we see artillery firing over our heads coming from the south, it could have been fired at a distance of ten to 20 kilometres. But whether they were at ten or 20 kilometres and, therefore, whether it would be impossible to see and hear artillery fired over your head from a shorter distance has not in any way established and therefore it is confusing. It is confusing me and it might confuse the witness as well. And it did not -- the sequence of questions you have not seriously considered the answer of the witness. We should clarify this, if he has any reason other than that it is possible to fire artillery from ten to 20 kilometres, whether he has any other reason to believe that there must have been at that distance and could not have been any closer because that is it the whole issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we please try to keep our -- seek clarity rather than mixing up matters and confusing matters. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, the document that you see before you, D85, has a range of an M63 of 8.6 kilometres. In the morning of the 4th of August, 1995, did you learn that morning or at any other time when you were gathering information about Operation Storm, that on the morning of the 4th, that the HV was firing from within 8.6 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, I did not, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In fact, sir, when you did your assessment -- let me rephrase that. When you did your assessment, did you conclude that the HV firing positions were approximately 20 kilometres away?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you make such an assessment when you were looking back at how Operation Storm was conducted?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't believe I ever did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, if you didn't, sir, did anybody else in the UN do it, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How about as part of the Canadian contingent?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Also not to my knowledge, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So your testimony, sir, is that -- I withdraw the question at this point. Now, the actual shelling that you and the other individuals counted was based on what you heard, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Part of it was based on what we heard directly going overhead of the camp and then explosions in the town and the area, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you an item that's in evidence, D741. And if I can have page 6 of that document. And this, I will tell you, Colonel, is the diary or translation of the diary of an ECMM official who was present at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, I would ask that we adhere to the same procedure we've done before if this is going to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, of course I have got no idea whether the matter Mr. Kehoe is drawing our attention to and drawing the attention of the witness to at this moment has been covered or not yet. If there's no question I -- we only can, of course, rely on Mr. Kehoe following the guidance of the Chamber. Mr. Kehoe, you're put on notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now the first sentence of this and he's talking about -- his diary in his house in Knin: "Today they're harvesting garlic in the kitchen below my terrace. You can hear sporadic shelling out of the Strmica during the morning." Now, from UN Sector South headquarters, did you in fact hear shelling -- well, let me withdraw that and just show you this document first which is P102, which is a situation report for the 4th of August, 1995. And Colonel, I would like to show you both of these before I ask any questions about this. As can you see this is a sitrep for 2000 hours on the 4th. If we can go to page 3 at the bottom of the page -- excuse me, all the way to the bottom of that page, if we can scroll down. Reports of KenBat. "There are total of 1230 bombreps, 638 ARSK, 592 HVO total." Now, at this particular juncture, sir, there was only one KenBat, observation post in operation and that was up around Strmica, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Strmica post was Kenyan Battalion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is -- yes. So this report by the Kenyan Battalion --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And just when I say KenBat this is the Kenyan Battalion who is reporting not -- as opposed to CanBat, Canadian Battalion. I know we have had some problem with that before, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the Kenyan Battalion is reporting 1230 bombreps from Strmica and my question to you, sir, is: When you're there in the camp, did you hear those impacts or that shelling taking place up in Strmica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If I can confirm one thing, Mr. Kehoe, what date are we talking about in this report?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is -- for clarity sake, so this is the 4th August and is a situation report --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can just go to the first page of this document in fairness to Colonel Williams. First page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's the first page of the document, Colonel. As you can see at the top, it is 4 August at 2000 hours.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Right, understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now my question to you again is that when you're sitting in UN Sector South could you hear this -- these bombreps that were being reported by the Kenyan Battalion during the 4th of August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: When there was artillery rounds firing or landing in Knin we could not; but when there was no sound in Knin from artillery fire, you could hear the echo of distant rounds, but that would be difficult to count. And I note that this goes up to 1800 hours on that day only, so it is not a full day report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Actually it is 2000 hour, I do believe, sir.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The one on UNMO Sector South daily says 1800, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We see that the date and time on which apparently this document was issued or sent is at 20 hours and the subject is Sector South daily sitrep with -- gives as the time 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm just trying to give the actual time that is on the document itself, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the witness says that, as he understands this document, that it covers the period until 1800 hours, which -- which seems fair to me. If it says that that's the subject even if it is written two hours later. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, also on the 4th, you were aware that there was shelling on the confrontation lines as well, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I would assume there would be, but I was not aware of exact numbers on the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you 1D55-0004. If you can blow this up just a bit. Just to orient you, Colonel, down below on the left-hand side is the map that you circled upon previously, which is now D928.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the information, Your Honour, from the confrontation lines that we have here is the -- derived from the information received by the Office of the Prosecutor in the war diary. And we've done is attempted to put these confrontation lines in various locales. These various peaks that are before you, Your Honour, are peaks in the mountains themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, taking a look at this particular map, in addition to shelling of Knin, there would, in fact, be shelling at various levels near the confrontation line, would there not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I've not seen this particular image before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us just take the first item which is the -- the ARSK defence line on the morning of the -- August the 5th at 5.00. Do you see that, sir, the red line?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The one that mentions Badanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now based on your analysis of the ARSK, they would have various levels of artillery support, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, they would, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the first level of artillery would be at the battalion level which is at the front line itself, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The second level of artillery support would be at the brigade level and that would be some distance back from the confrontation line, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If the intent was to stay there and fight, that's correct, sir, it would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And lastly, sir, there is generally an operational level, which is back yet further from the brigade, to support the battalions and the brigades. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: In a situation where this was displayed as you're saying, that's correct. It would be there to support in areas where the attack or defence is faltering, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In addition to these three levels, you also have, in a simple logistics analysis, roads leading up to these various levels, be it at the battalion or the brigade or the operational level, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: You would have roads that would be dedicated in priority to the brigade or to the battalion depending on the particular usage, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Colonel on the morning of the 4th, a commander who wanted to attack the enemy would be shelling all three of these levels, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If a commander wanted to attack an opposing army he thought would fight, they would shell these areas to deny him access to the town, if that's what you're getting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And how many soldiers and artillery pieces did your intelligence reflect that the ARSK had at these three levels?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't recall those numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us move to the next morning, which is the 5th. And without asking the same questions, as the ARSK is pushed back and the war diary reflects this second confrontation line, you would still have this three levels of artillery support at this confrontation line as well, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: You would have still have the three levels of artillery support if the defence had not collapsed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can I just make a clarification? I'm -- it's unclear to me whether or not the witness is being asked what in general would be done, should be done in his opinion a reasonable commander or army would do, or what he has specific information actually was done on the 4th and 5th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Kehoe was clear in his questions that he is asking what would be done and he is not referring to -- he may suggest that that was done, but that is not his question. Even -- of course, in the answers we find some additional information, for example, the use of artillery. The witness answered the question by saying if a commander wanted to attack an opposing army, well, that of course then would be a condition for the things he said and we should not forget that that was part of his answer. Please proceed. You could even ask whether the witness -- what the witness observed, whether he considered this to be an attack by the ARSK on an opposing army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The HV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Or the HV, I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is exactly what we are we're talking about. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just taking, Colonel, Mr. Russo's suggestion, on the 4th, was the HV shelling these various artillery support positions that had been set up by the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge. I also have no knowledge of what ARSK artillery positions remained on the 4th of August, if any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So if we go back just briefly from this document, and we don't need it to go back on the screen, in P102, in the sitrep that you correctly pointed out was from 1800 on the 4th, and we had 638 bombreps by the ARSK, as an intelligence officer do you have any idea where the ARSK was firing those 638 artillery reps from or bombreps from?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I do not have any knowledge where they were firing from them, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we'll offer into evidence 1D55-0004 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D814.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D814 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us go to -- to the specific shelling that you observed, and if I can bring back up P928. Just as a reference point, sir, looking at the locations of P928 and focussing on the red and blue items, those are items where you testified that you observed shells impacting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I can turn to 1D55-0016. And for -- if we can spin that, please. Your Honour, for references purposes, this is an extract from D131, which is an item that we've discussed previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I have not forgotten about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I say that for Your Honours' purposes but also for the purposes of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... no, no, it is appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now looking at this, Colonel, you would agree with me that the shelling that you observed, if we can just look at this -- first at the D1 area, that was the shelling you identified at the Tvik factory. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I would say approximately. And I also note that this image is at least 13 years newer than the previous image, so there may be some construction that's not actually there at the time I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I appreciate that, sir.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But that's in the Tvik factory, and D2 being the supply Agroprerada depot?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The other place that you identified, if we can move down to the area around, you identified some areas around B1. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I take it from your statement that -- excuse me, from your clarification statement that you didn't know where the ARSK headquarters were?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And for reference purposes, Your Honour, what I'm referring to is the last page of his supplemental sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Likewise, sir, the -- you also indicated some areas around -- if I can look -- locate this. You noted the RSK parliament area which is B8?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But you didn't know -- did you know that there was RSK TV in that area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I did not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You noted for us as well the area around the railroad junction which is E10?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, that of course was the railway junction that one would take out so that they couldn't move on that railway junction. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So basically the areas that you observed being hit, sir, as an intelligence officer you would conclude were military targets, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I would conclude that those were military targets in lines with the laws of armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You are familiar with the concept of dual use for facilities, are you not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I am, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And let me turn your attention to D718.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I will offer into evidence 1D55-0016.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D815, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D815 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Once again my apologies, Your Honour, for moving too quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The risk is that it will not be admitted, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand. If I can turn to page 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, just looking at this, sir, if you see the point A 4 in this document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: A4, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you aware, on the morning of the 4th, for instance, that -- that this school had been used as a mortar position?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was unaware of that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How about A6 which is the elementary school. Do you see that, sir? A6 right in the centre of the page. Just look to the right of A4.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: A6, I see. I apologise. I'm not as easily able to familiarize myself with this image because it is a lot newer than the Knin I'm familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, sir. Heaven knows, everybody in this courtroom's been looking at these maps a lot more frequently than we care to talk about.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, that's not it, sir. It's -- this is a 2007 image. I'm used to looking Knin from 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, sir.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just the location of A6, if we may?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I see it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now in that elementary school, were you aware that there was an ARSK unit garrisoned at that location?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm not aware that that is a possibility, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you are likewise familiar with the concept of mobile targets, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And mobile targets being soldiers or --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Columns of armoured vehicle, moving soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Or even a single vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: A single military vehicle, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now from your position in the UN Sector South balcony, were you aware of units of ARSK soldiers moving around the Knin area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was unaware of units moving around the Knin area, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let me just touch on a topic that you noted for, and I think you addressed it with Mr. Russo, concerning harassment fire. Now, you said that there were individual rounds that were -- two or three that were going off through the course of the day and you determined that that was harassment fire. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you recall you and I meeting on the 16th of August of last year, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I recall us meeting in Ottawa, sir, last year, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yeah. And did you not tell me that with regard to that shelling, you didn't know if it was harassment, it is hard to say. Don't know if it was harassment or going after other targets.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It could be either, sir, and my assessment was it could be harassment fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So as you sit here, you're telling us it could be harassment fire or could be HV going after other targets?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If, as you said, sir, we're talking about mobile targets, yes, it could be HV going after mobile targets. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And as you sit here, you don't know if it is one or the other?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I could not with 100 percent certainty say whether it was mobile targets or harassment fire, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, turning back to the 4th, you chronicle in Exhibit 744 the comings and goings of Captain Berikoff?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I note at 8.00 on the morning of the 4th, you note that: "Captain Berikoff returns from town." Do you know what he was doing there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm just trying to find the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. It's 744. I'm not sure what tab it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, could you help us out with that, on 744.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: The last tab in his sheets.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. What time are we looking at, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just the second page at 8.00 in the morning. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Where it says: "Captain Berikoff returns from town."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: What was he doing in town?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He was there on reconnaissance to find out what activity was going on in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what did that entail, did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was he there by himself or was he there with somebody else? What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't know if he was with somebody else. I would assume he would be because we tended not to by -- our rules was not to travel alone, but I cannot confirm that, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask what "recce" stands for?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's reconnaissance. They call it -- the military lingo for recce is just short for reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Later on that day, at -- at 10.10 you have -- Captain Berikoff going to the hospital with the SMEDLO. And two lines down, returning on -- at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What was the purpose of that; do you know?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Captain Berikoff had gone with the Senior Medical Officer to see if there was any assistance that could be rendered by the Czechs who were our medical personnel in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You were reporting this back to CanCon as we see in 1225 insert?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Why was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: We tried to give them as accurate a picture as we understood at the time, back to our higher headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At that point, Colonel, did you and the other people in Sector South begin to discuss with CanCon taking wounded ARSK soldiers into the compound?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did -- did that ever come up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did that ever come up, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did at any point on the 4th or the 5th, did you take wounded ARSK soldiers into UN Sector South?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Go to the insert for 2300 on the 4th.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: By 2300, you had already taken the refugee population into UN Sector South. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Not at 2300, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, the last sentence here: "Two ARSK officers arrived to discuss request for refugee protection." Who were these ARSK officers you talk about?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Who were they, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't know their names. They arrived to talk to General Forand who was at the gate at that time. I requested that he come to the gate so that we could deal with the refugee situation. At that same time, the Krajina Serb officers arrived. I have no idea who they were or what they talked about with General Forand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, did General Forand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you ever informed as to why -- what went on in this discussion between General Forand and these ARSK officers who came to the gate at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, 1400 on 744, if you can. It notes, briefing to staff. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now you were also briefing G2, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, one of the people that you were talking with during the course of the day was an individual by the name of Theunens, wasn't it, who was up in G2 in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what was his role in Zagreb at G2?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He worked in the United Nations headquarters. He was a Belgian officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And at what time on the 4th did you begin to talk to Mr. Theunens in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact time, sir. I know at times we did not have communications with anything outside of Knin. We could not contact Zagreb. I don't recall the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Have you been made aware that Mr. Theunens works for the Office of the Prosecutor now?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I had no idea, sir. That is the first time I am hearing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During the course of the day on the 4th -- let me withdraw that. How many times during the course of the day on the 4th did you talk to Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I cannot recall talking to him more than once. I know I talked to the Canadian contingent once and Canada once. I don't recall any more than that, sir. I don't recall any more than that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During the course of the day when you were talking to the individuals in Zagreb, did you talk to an individual by the name of Joakim Robertsson?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't recall talking to Joakim Robertsson, no. I believe there's an individual called Joakim Robertsson who was an investigator who I talked to afterwards in August or September, but I don't recall talking to him that day, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let us begin to discuss the evening of the 4th and going into the 5th. And in your supplemental statement, you note in the last paragraph of your supplemental statement, P927: "Mr. Williams stated that given that the lack of defence in Knin, he does not believe that there was a military necessity to shell the military targets in Knin particularly on 5 August when the HV should have known there was no defence in the town." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I see that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us talk about that. Now, preliminarily, you knew, sir, as you said previously, that Operation Storm was an operation that was by the HV in both Sector North and Sector South.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Our assessment was there would be an assault on the Krajina at Sector South and North simultaneously. We were not aware of any Croat plan or Croat operation name, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you also -- and you also knew that the headquarters for the army of the Republic of Serb Krajina was located in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: We knew the headquarters was located in Knin, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you also knew that any successful battle against the ARSK needed -- any success in the battle needed to bring about some damage or destruction to the communication compatibilities of the ARSK and their command structure. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: In order to defeat an enemy, yes, sir, that would be one way of doing it. Destroying their command structure, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us just talk a little bit about what you wrote in your report at 1715 on the 4th. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You reflect in your report that the ARSK reports 200 HV deaths.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. From the Radio Knin reporting we spoke about earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Without going into the number, at the time, Colonel, you -- without staying with 200, you knew that as of the evening of the 4th, that the HV sustained quite a few casualties, didn't they, be they wounded or dead?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: We didn't have exact figures, sir, but we assumed and assessed that they would have sustained a fair number of casualties, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And let me turn your attention to P698. This is a report by Captain Dangerfield who was a Sector Liaison Officer in UN Sector South. This is his report as of the 4th of August. And let me just -- do you know Captain Dangerfield, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have met Captain Dangerfield, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And let me just review with you his report, beginning on paragraph 2: "It was a long time before HV HVO made any headway on the ground. In the early afternoon, the picture began to develop and we saw five main areas of attack." And he notes the various areas of attack and the axes. Let us turn to the next page, paragraph 10. Paragraph 10, SLO assessment for 5 August 1995. "Saturday, 05 August should see another initial heavy artillery barrage of HV objectives. G2 assessment is that Knin may fall by dark on 05 August."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "In order to do so, I believe that the HV will require a more successful day than today. Troops approaching from the south face a stiff opposition." Now, before we move on, was that your assessment as well that troops moving from the south, as they came in on the 4th, were going to face a stiff opposition?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No sir. My assessment was the one line saying: Due to assessment, Knin may fall by dark 05 August." The rest I would believe to be his assessment, though I have not seen Captain Dangerfield's report before today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you disagree with him?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of his vantage point, what he is seeing at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know how long Captain Dangerfield spent in the Knin area prior to you getting there on the 3rd?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I do not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "SLO recces last week saw considerable evidence of road use by ARSK tracked vehicles." Were you aware of that, sir, of the ARSK moving tracked vehicles the prior week?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me, again, just object. This procedure seems to be getting flipped all of the time. Mr. Williams should have been asked first what his information was and then be confronted with what Mr. Dangerfield said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is the guidance the Chamber gave, so if we are talking about track vehicles then we could ask the witness before we put to him what Mr. Dangerfield has testified. Please proceed. Or has reported, I should say. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, were you aware that, in the prior week, that UN personnel had seen evidence of track vehicles ARSK track vehicles?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the information in Captain Dangerfield's report, no, sir, reference to track vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Here again, Mr. Kehoe, the right procedure would be whether the witness had seen it; if he had not seen it, whether he was aware that others had seen it and then put to him -- Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, did you observe a considerable presence of ARSK forces in the area on the 4th and the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I did not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to the next page. So did anybody in UN Sector South inform you that there was a considerable presence of ARSK forces in the area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So if we look at paragraph 12: "While Knin may come under heavy attack again, the considerable presence of ARSK forces in the area will require more time before they come under direct fire from HV tanks." So this particular assessment of the considerable presence of ARSK forces by Captain Dangerfield, is it your testimony that you disagree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I can't comment on his assessment because I didn't have access to the facts that Captain Dangerfield had, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say, Colonel, that Captain Dangerfield had more information than you did upon which to make this assessment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If the information he has in his report is accurate, sir, I have no reason to doubt that -- or I have no way to confirm it, then I would say he had access to more information than I did, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was it your assessment at the time, Colonel, that there was either two options available at the end of the day on the 4th: Surrender by the ARSK and President Martic; or a -- for lack of a better term, bloody last stand in Knin? Was that your assessment on the evening of the 4th?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't believe so, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to paragraph 15. "The request for aid to evacuation women and children, leaving behind ARSK troops only, shows signs of a disturbing final showdown. With the advancing HV/HVO troops looking at Knin as their final objective and ARSK troops remaining. Milan Martic will have to surrender or face a bloody last stand in the capital of Krajina."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Right, sir, and I see that as Captain Dangerfield's conclusion or assessment of one of the potential courses of action for the Republika Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And my question for you is: Did you see those as the two options that were confronting the ARSK on the evening of the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I believe that question has already been asked and already been answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, that seems to be the case. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, as part of your intelligence gathering, were you aware that the ARSK was withdrawing troops for the direct defence of the Knin on the evening of the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand. When you say withdrawing are you indicating from a specific location or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, could you please try to make it two questions, whether they were withdrawing and whether the witness is aware of the purposes of this withdrawal. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On the evening of the 4th of August, were the ARSK -- did they begin to withdraw from their front line positions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Are we talking specifically within Knin, sir? Or within Sector North and South.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's just talk about Sector South.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Sector South; very good, sir. No specific knowledge that they were withdrawing from positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you ever learn in your intelligence gathering that General Mrksic had ordered forces to withdraw from various -- any position to -- for the defence of Knin?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was not aware that General Mrksic had actually ordered a withdrawal of that. So I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you D106. This is a transcript from a radio report, 2330 hours on the 4th with Belgrade Radio. Now my first question with regard to this document, Colonel, is this: If you had learned that General Mrksic was in contact with Radio Belgrade on the evening of the 4th that, of course, would indicate to you that the HV was unsuccessful in completely eliminating the ARSK's communication capabilities. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't believe I could say that as far as completely eliminating. The fact that the General could talk to Radio Belgrade would mean he had some forms of communication, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And let me look down about five lines. The question is: "Does that mean our lines have been penetrated?" General Mrksic answers: "No. We are maintaining contact. Our forces withdrew to positions for the direct defence of Knin?" Now, your testimony is that you did not learn about that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But you did say, sir, that on the morning of the 5th, and let me flip back to P744, on the morning of the 5th at 6.10, ARSK tanks and one BOV, one truck, heading south to north through Knin. I don't want to get ahead of you, Colonel, but do you see that on the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That was -- so what you observed was a mechanized unit on the move?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you again another portion of this Sekulic book. And by the way, you saw this going from south to north.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Than would have been from the direction of Drnis, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Drnis is to the south of Knin, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to 1D44-0119.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, this is a portion of this book, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How large is the portion?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, one portion I have is -- if I could just have one moment just for a little clarity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can call 1D44-0003. The English is 1D44-0119. And the B/C/S is 1D44-0029.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think that is already admitted as Exhibit D813.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Is that not what was admitted earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, it's a different portion, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Beginning on the page with -- this is on the 4th of August again, General Sekulic's book: "At 2000 hours a meeting was held at the Main Staff operation centre. Attended by 7th Corps Brigade commanders and the Corps commander, Slobodan Kovacevic. The meeting was chaired by the commander of the army of the Serbian Krajina Main Staff, General Mile Mrksic." If we could just move down three lines. "Commander Mrksic's position that the evacuation was a matter for the authorities indicates that the army ought to continue with defence and facilitate the evacuation of the population." Skipping a sentence: "In order to defend Knin "--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have a look at what page we are exactly at this moment in the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is page 24 of the book, but it's 1D44 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, that seems to be the translation. I'm looking at the book itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The original.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the B/C/S it is 180.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 180 is in evidence as D813, as Mr. Russo said, Mr. Kehoe. That's a 93-page document, and it is page 27 out of the 93. That is at least what my computer tells me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have been informed, Judge, that with regard to this, that we were invited by the Chamber to make an excerpt out of this which we have attempted to do at this juncture. I mean, we will take the Court's guidance and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but then it has not yet been uploaded. What is at this moment in the e-court system is still the whole of the document under number D813. That is, 93 pages. No, if Mr. Russo says so and you say, no, it's not the case, then perhaps it might be worthwhile to verify perhaps for a second and see whether there's any merit in what he says, as there appears to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is a chance that there is a backlog in updating. If that is case, I totally, without good cause, ask you at this occasion to listen to Mr. Russo, which doesn't mean that you should not now and then listen to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I always listen to Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but apparently as it appears --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My guiding light.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- it appears to be still in the system, but it may be for other reasons that, although you have reduced the size of D813, that is not yet in our system. And to the extent I was not fully informed about this backlog, I apologise for addressing you as I did. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, if we could get back and continue to take a look at this item, if we may. Beginning with that sentence you see in the order to defend Knin?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "In order to defend Knin, the commander of the army of the Serbian Krajina Main Staff ordered the commander of the 7th Corps, General Kovacevic, to pull a battalion out of the 75th Brigade by morning and deploy it in positions for the defence of Knin at Bulina Strana." If we go down skipping that one paragraph to the next beginning item, sentence on the next paragraph: "Chief of operations department went to Drnis to the 75th Brigade command and Commander Vladimir Davidovic to speed up the dispatch of a battalion to Bulina Strana Sector North of Knin." Now you know, Colonel, based on your function in G2 that the 75th Brigade, the two digits, two numbers, 7-5, that was a mechanized brigade which had tanks and APCs. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The 75th Brigade had mechanized -- as a mech brigade would have tanks and armoured personnel carriers, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And as we see from the other -- that paragraph that it was supposed to be done by the morning that would be the morning of the 5th?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And likewise, that Commander Davidovic was to deploy them to Bulina Strana. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now. You were also aware that the position of certainly UN Sector South at this time, that the Croats were not in direct fire range of Knin as of the evening of the 4th, were they?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, based on -- if you were in the position -- let me say this. Let me show first before I ask you a question. Let me show you 1D55-0004.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I move on I will tender this -- this page which is 1D44-000 -- 0119 in the English, which is 1D44-0029 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, no objection. Let me just now -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now let us go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we're now talking about same book, different page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is just one page is sufficient for the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit D816, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D816 is admitted into evidence. It is only now, Mr. Russo, that I became aware that when you said D813 I was sufficiently thinking about that that was exactly the document on which the Defence was invited to reduce the size. So the observation at that time that it was already in evidence, of course, did not assist much because we all knew that Mr. Kehoe would limit the size of that portion and it might well outside of the limited portion he would choose. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't mean to repeat the same issue. I think this is actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But not necessarily the part that will remain in D813.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: This next exhibit is D814. I believe it is the Google Earth images which were called up and admitted earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have seen this picture before, Mr. Kehoe, that's for --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the wrong number. Let's get to the right number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now the area of Bulina Strana, do you see that on the map, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Are you familiar with that area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have been by that area once. I'm not overly familiar but I have passed by there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the Bulina Strana area is the high ground in that locale, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Just in that direction from Knin, yes, it's, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, sir, based on -- well, let just look at these particular locations. You saw a mechanized unit at 6.00 in the morning travelling from Drnis, pass the camp and into Knin out of your sight line. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You don't know, as you sit here, whether or not that mechanized unit was deployed as we saw in the order by General Mrksic to Bulina Strana or not, do you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I do not know if that unit was deployed as ordered by General Mrksic to Bulina Strana. You're correct, sir, I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If a mechanized unit was deployed to Bulina Strana, or if any troops were deployed to Bulina Strana as reflected on that, they would have a high ground location upon which to fire into Knin, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If they were deployed, yes, they would, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in addition to that, on the morning or throughout the day on the 5th, did you receive reports from, for instance, the Canadian Battalion that there were ARSK mechanized units or other pieces of equipment moving towards Knin?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't recall receiving reports, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to D124. This is a sitrep of the 5th of August, the dating on it is 1700. Excuse me, 1900. And correct me if I'm wrong, Colonel, but it reflects information up to 1800 on the 4th or -- 1800 on the 4th until 1800 on the 5th. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, but you're asking me if I received a report from the Canadian Battalion. This is an UNMO sector report. I'm confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to reference you and orient you, Colonel. I'm going to take to --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could go four pages in to the CanBat AOR. As we're doing that, just again you referenced this mechanized -- ARSK mechanized unit moving at 6.10 on the 5th.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can go to CanBat -- that's the Canadian Battalion, not the Kenyan Battalion. If we can go one page back, please. This is some entries, sir, from the Canadian Battalion.
