Some of them are clearer than others, frankly, and certainly if can you move at 0530 on August the 5th. You see: "Vehicles moving toward the general direction of Knin." If we move down on that page, you can see another reference of vehicles moving towards Knin. And, likewise, some on the next page. Were you made aware during the day on the 5th that the ARSK was moving units and it looked like from the reporting that they were headed towards Knin?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was made aware there was ARSK movements. I was not made aware they were formed units or whether they were stragglers. I have not seen this report, that does mean the headquarters received it. I can't confirm that we actually received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You can't confirm that you actually received it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Actually received this report. Our communications were iffy, to say the best, for the 4th and 5th of August. But I have not seen this report, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Obviously you have no reason to doubt the accuracy of what the Canadian Battalion is reporting.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have no way nor no reason to doubt their accuracy, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, based on what you told us or what we discussed, obviously communication capabilities had not been knocked out by the HV. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Whose communications facilities are you referring to, sir? The Krajina Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The Krajina Serbs.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have no way of confirming that but it would appear there was still some functioning communications. The vehicles were still moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you at least observed ARSK movements, although you didn't know where they were going, in Knin. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, sir, as a military commander, do you recall when we discussed this matter on the 16th of August of last year that you noted on the 5th when asked why you assessed that they would shell on the morning of the 5th, that you would have shelled Knin too. Because if there was any ARSK resistance, you might want to have them change their mind about resistance?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So as you sit here, sir, if you were in the position of General Gotovina, you would have shelled Knin also on the morning of the 5th?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm not sure what reports General Gotovina would have had back from his forces in contact from the results of his artillery and the attack. But he may not have had a full picture either, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But the answer to that question is, you would have shelled too?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I cannot speak for what General Gotovina knew of the actual situation on the ground, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm speaking for you, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I, as an intelligence officer, am not in a command position, sir. I'm an advisor to the commander. I don't wish to be evasive and I'm not intending to do so. I'm just saying I don't know what General Gotovina had knowledge-wise of the situation in Knin that day, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, when you and I discussed this on the 16th of August last year, did you or did not tell me that you would have shelled Knin on the morning of the 5th as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Depending upon the picture I had, that's right, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't know if you'd want to take a break now, Judge, I know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'd like to take a break. Could you tell us how much more time you'd need.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just gather myself here just a bit and give you an accurate assessment after the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you already could give it a try so that we can think it over as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We use our break as well to consider whether we would grant what you think you would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I can finish by 7.00 if the break is not too long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider. Could I hear from the other parties how much time they would need. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have no questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've got about a half an hour, at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we'll have a break, not too short. Mr. Kehoe, by the way, there is one other issue which I'd like to raise. You have shown 1D55-0004 to the witness which was a picture and then you'd shown it to the witness. It was on the screen. It was admitted as D814. And of course at that moment I had not verified that there was a second page attached to that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which gives different information, et cetera, and apparently, by chance, you called D814 at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I thought it was two pages. I thought it was two separate documents as opposed to one document. That was my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because we're trying to do our utmost best to keep a close eye on what comes in as evidence and what not. If you just show one thing to a witness and then we're not going as a routine checking whether there's anything hidden behind this one page, so would you please be very precise on that. We'll have a break and resume at a quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you have until 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, let me turn your attention to 65 ter 4077 -- excuse me, 4022. If we can go to the first page. This is an UNCRO headquarters Zagreb document as of the 7th. As you can see from paragraph 1 it is an assessment of the attitude and likely reasons of the defeat of the ARSK.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I see that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Number 2, it says: "Resistance offered by ARSK has been in most case a frontal blocking action that has proved successful to some extent in Sector North but rapidly overwhelmed in Sector South." Now when you were going back and doing this assessment, Sector North didn't fall to the HV until Knin fell. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct. But I'd just like to clarify which assessment are you referring to, sir. My after the fact assessment? This assessment is not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand. I'm just talking about your after the fact assessment --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Understood, sir. Thank you. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page. Paragraph 4 for the most part: "The rapid collapse of the ARSK after the initial breakthrough can be explained as follows: 41, poor leadership at intermediate levels has been observed. 42, absence of a counterattack reserve (armour has been observed only on the first echelon. 43: Lack of theatre, C 3 I, capacities and leaders were not trained for coordinated theatre-level ops; 44, logistic insufficiencies. 45, rapid demoralization of troops. I want to turn your attention back to 43, total lack of theatre, C 3 I. Now, C 3 I is the military short for command, control, communication, and intelligence. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And one of the reasons why the ARSK fell so quickly, and now I'm talking about your after the fact assessment, fell so quickly was because their communication capabilities from Knin were destroyed on the 4th and the 5th. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, I want to change subjects. I'm just trying to get through this, Colonel, and I trust I won't go through it too quickly for you, and if I do, please stop me.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I will, and I thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I want to turn to the actual mortar situation on the 5th that you talked about. And we talked about the movement of a mechanized unit to Bulina Strana in the previous documents, and if you can turn to 744, P744, I'm sorry. It should be the last tab in your book.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Which page, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's on the fifth -- on 1500, sir, of P744.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Right, I have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Should be the fourth page in. It notes that: "ARSK soldiers of unknown strength were seen occupying defensive positions in the general area of Strmica." This particular defensive position, do you know when the ARSK took up this defensive position?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I do not, sir. This reporting is from our Kenyan Battalion which had a border check-point in Strmica. I don't have any further information, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As I said, we talked about Bulina Strana and we have this insert about the defensive positions in and around Strmica. How many other defensive positions, to your knowledge, did the ARSK set up in and around Knin on the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: None others to my knowledge. I was surprised they did not set up one to block crossing across the bridge into Knin, but none other to my knowledge, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Not to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I guess that you -- and as we talked about before, you were unaware of the Bulina Strana situation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. I was unaware of that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, as we look -- given what we've talked about the mortar attack shell that landed near the base on the 9th of August, you don't know who fired that, do you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Sorry, sir. Which mortar attack are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm talking to the mortars that killed the individuals at the cross-roads.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. You're talking about on the 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On the 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... sorry, I was thinking the 9th of August I was gone. I don't know who fired that, sir, you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if we could just go through some of the people and if we could pull up P220 again, which is the UNMO document -- excuse me, the UNCIVPOL report that Mr. Russo discussed with you. Now, if we can start with the last person first, number 6, the male?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That was the individual who obviously had been dead for some time and rigor mortis had set in?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't know if rigor mortis had set in, but the blood was certainly not fresh blood. It was more burgundy in colour as opposed to crimson.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And did you conclude, based on that, that that body had been brought there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So that body, you deduced, was killed prior to this mortar landing?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm not a forensic expert, sir, but that's what I deduced, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now the first person that you talk about on this is Ljubomir Djapic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Ljubomir Djapic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He is the individual that you took out of -- whose ID you took out, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now when you came on the scene with Captain Berikoff and others, Mr. Djapic was dead, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn you to -- if I may. 1D55-0019. Excuse me, 1D55-0009. My apology, 009. Colonel, this is the -- I will tell you based on the records that are currently in evidence that this is the autopsy report for Mr. Djapic. And you can look at that but we can scroll down and the determination of the cause of death is a gunshot wound to the head?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we will offer into evidence 1D55-0009.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no objection. I believe this may one of the documents which has been submitted by the Prosecution on the killings bar table motion, but, of course, we have no objection to the submission of this document. Just want to keep that in mind for further indication on those exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At the risk of duplication, Judge, we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is one page that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- I can confer with counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. Let's not -- it is now tendered by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And therefore, there's no objection. Madam Registrar, that would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit D817, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, may I then take it that you will remove it from your bar table motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: We will do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, so if this individual was killed from a gunshot wound he, likewise, was dead prior to the mortar landing in the morning of the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If autopsy says that, sir, I have no reason to doubt that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The other individual that you mentioned to us, which was the number 2. Now number 2 on -- on -- if we can go back to P220. So just looking at this list, again, with one and six being killed prior to the mortar attack. Number two is the individual who came to the UN Sector South gate and attempted to get in. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... been informed that the Prosecution has led evidence in that regard, that the individual who has -- came to the gate and was turned away was killed in this mortar attack?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I'm going to object to the form of that question. If he wants to point to the particular witness who said it and address him way. I'm not sure what the purpose of asking him if he is aware --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: -- of what the Prosecution has led.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... led as evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I think that that's -- we're not -- rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will take Mr. Russo's suggestion again and turn the Chamber's attention to Captain Berikoff's testimony at page 755, line 9, by Mr. Russo. "Question: There it indicates that a scared ARSK soldier came to the gate," it says of the UNHCR, but UNHCR compound, "and that he was turned away." First of all, can you tell the Court whether you were the one who turned him away?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was the one who turned this young man away. I was the one who spoke to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, can I just finish Captain Berikoff's --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My question -- I was reading when I said: "First -- first of all, can you tell the Court whether you were the one who turned him away?" And that's a question by Mr. Russo to Captain Berikoff.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I apologise. I thought you were directing the question to me, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Answer by Captain Berikoff: "Yes. I was the one who turned him away." Sounds familiar. "He came to the gate along with a number of other refugees, but because he was in uniform and he was carrying a weapon, we were ordered by our senior management that we were not allowed to let combatants into the compound so I turned him away at that time." Question by Mr. Russo: "Thank you. And was this soldier that you turned away, one of the soldiers killed at the mortar blast at the intersection? " Answer: "Yes, he was." Now, as you sit here, Colonel, do you disagree with the assessment of the situation given by Captain Berikoff?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: With regards to this particular individual, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, how many soldiers were in the six people who were killed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Of the six that were killed, two were in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention, Chamber to Captain Berikoff, page 7588, line 9. And looking at this question and looking -- by Mr. Russo looking at the second entry for 930 Bravo, it indicates that of the six dead at the intersection where the mortar blast occurred, four were civilians and two were ARSK soldiers. However, I believe your other references indicate that it was the other way around, four soldiers and two civilians. Is that right?" "Answer: That's correct. It was in fact four soldiers and two civilians." Now, Colonel, do you disagree with Mr. Berikoff's assessment of that situation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I disagree with his assessment. There were two individuals in uniform and four civilians. I can't explain for the discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You noted for us that you -- during the course of your testimony you saw this individual that had been shot in the back of the head?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you recall you and I discussing that on the 16th of August of last year?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And did you tell me at that time that that individual did not appear that he was executed. He did have an AK-47.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He had an AK-47 and there was a gunshot to the back of the head. I don't know if he was executed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My question to you is: Did you tell me back on the 16th that you had concluded that you did not think he was executed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't recall, sir. If you say I did, I have no reason to doubt you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, a couple of other questions briefly, sir, as we move through this. Now, with the situation of warlords that you were asked on direct examination, were you -- were you made aware during the course of your intelligence gathering of any criminal elements in the Krajina after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: None?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me show you a report, which is P805. And I would like to show you this report. This is -- P805, sir, is a report an ECMM report from the 7th of August, 1995. If I can turn to the second page towards the bottom of this page 2. And I recognise, Colonel, that you may have seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have not seen this document before, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I just want to -- there is a piece of information here that I'd just like to get to your attention. On the B -- and this is on the subject of looting. "In the Knin --" 5 b at the bottom: "In the Knin area, it seems as if random looting and destruction of houses and property is about to reach a degree where it will get even more difficult to restart normal life. Comment: It is it a very unlikely that this is a deliberate policy of the authorities. It is more likely that as the front line more disciplined troops are moving out, the second line soldiers are less disciplined and are more ready to grab what they can." Now, my first question is: During the course of my conversation with you in August of last year, you stated at that time that the looting that you observed did not appear to be organised. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you, likewise, said that most of this looting was done by Home Guards?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that some of the looters had patches, some were wearing BDUs or fatigues, is that right, BDUs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Some had no patches, some had fatigues on and some did not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So it was a mixture of people with uniforms, out of uniforms, without patches, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's right, sir. The bulk were in uniform but there some were without, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And based on that all, you concluded that this looting was not organised?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It did not appear to me, from what I saw, that it was organised or sanctioned looting, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you noted in 744 at 1445 on the August 7th. And let me -- P744, I think that is tab 4 in your book. At 1445, you note that the -- lots of troops getting ready to leave. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, I'm still trying to find that, sir. I'm at tab 4. That's the supplemental --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm looking for your Sector South chronology?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Very last tab.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Mr. Russo. Page 6 of P744.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have it now, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At the insert for 1445. You note that a lot of soldiers and trucks getting ready to leave. Do you see that? At 1445?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, I'm still trying to find --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you look on the screen that might be of help. The second one from the top on the screen, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you also -- if we scroll down to the next page -- actually the bottom of this page for August the 10th. On August the 10th, you note that there's still fighting in the area of Strmica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's the reporting we had, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay and, likewise, go to the next page. You have fighting on the 13th, the 14th. So throughout that period of time, your reporting was that the -- there was still serious fighting going on between the HV and the ARSK, or certainly Serb forces, immediately following Operation Storm. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There was still some fighting going on, sir. I'm not sure if I would categorise it as serious. The reporting was -- there were gaps in reporting. But, yes, there was still fighting going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's go to D728. Page 11 of D728. If we can go to the next page, please. Now, your reporting reflect, Colonel, that -- if you see the box in the top, a confrontation line being reset at the conclusion of Storm that looked like this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: As you've mentioned before, I have not seen this slide show before but I would have to say that looks fairly accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we go to the next page. Did your reporting also reflect these counter-strikes by the Serb forces in and around the 12th? I can show you the next slide as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can go to the next slide, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Which shows the counterattack by the forces of the Split Military District. Now, Colonel, after the -- Operation Storm ended, and the confrontation line moved up to the area that we discussed previously, the HV went into a mode of setting out an active defence didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I would assess that that's what they did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And explain to the Chamber what an active defence is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: An active defence, in my understanding, would be they were respond if attacked and defend in the positions they were in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now based on that, do you also try to probe various areas to get a better defensive position while also looking and trying to plan where you can actually have an offensive?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. In the conduct of a campaign would you probe the defences whether it be by reconnaissance or actively fighting for information. Doctrinally, that's what you would do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, during this period of active defence, if you're planning a -- a next offensive, what is a commander such as General Gotovina, what is he doing during this period of time to control the active defence and also plan the next offensive operation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If I was a commander in that position, I would make sure that my main supply routes up to the new defence line would be secure and I would make sure there was no resistance in my rear lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And how about logistics, sir? What would you do logically in order to prepare or to take care of not only your active defence but also to prepare for the next offensive?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I would conduct resupply if it was my decision. I am sure he would do the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Based on your intelligence, the active defence was set up almost immediately after Operation Storm. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I can't confirm that, when exactly it was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you D281. This is an order for active defence signed by General Gotovina as of the 9th of August, 1995. If we can go to the next page. Without going into the specifics of the order, because obviously we don't have that kind of time, was this consistent with what information you were receiving i.e., that General Gotovina was ordering his troops into an active defence with the idea of planning for subsequent offensives?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: As you mentioned, I have not seen the document before. I would assess and our assessment at that time was that this is something that General Gotovina would do, establish gains he had made to get ready for the next part of the campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now let us go back to D728, if we may. And if we can go to page 14. Actually, 15. 15, if we may. One more, please. I must have counted incorrectly. Now, based on your intelligence gathering, Colonel, the next step was Operation Mistral. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: We were not aware at the time of the name of the operation. But this slide I have not seen before and it looks very much like the Dayton Peace Accord, but I know it is it not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn to the next page then. It is reminiscent of that, isn't it? Now, you recall this operation, even if you don't recall the name of the offensive, going into Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I recall this offensive, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, you assessed at that time that this was an extensive operation that took a tremendous amount of planning as well as logistical support; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Planning, logistical support and coordination between the HV and HVO, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You're a career officer, Colonel. I mean, would you give us an idea of the time and energy involved in such an endeavour planning such an endeavour?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Planning such an endeavour involving different forces geographically disparate in the terrain such as the HV and HVO were fighting would certainly take a number of weeks and even that would be quick.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you put that in conjunction with putting an active defence in place, there is an significant amount of activity on the plate of a commander to complete all these tasks, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, sir, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As we move through the fall and we need not go through the rest of the slides, your assessment was that though September, October, into the end of these operations, General Gotovina was the commander of the HV forces and HVO forces operating in conjunction with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina throughout all this, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That was our assessment, sir, but we didn't have clarification that that was a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can just put up on the screen 65 ter 3327. This is just a 65 ter document, General Gotovina requesting General Cermak not to send internationals into the zone until further notice. Colonel, I know you haven't seen this document before --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- but we will offer this document into evidence at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D818, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D818 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Lastly, Judge, I failed to offer into evidence 65 ter 4022, which is the UNCRO sitrep of the 7th of August, 1995, that I discussed with the Colonel previously and I would offer that at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D819, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D819 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, I have no further questions for you. I thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Before we continue, you asked us to admit into evidence D817, the autopsy report. Now, it seems that it's not just an autopsy report but it's more than that. It is a seven-page document which is, to some extent not translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is -- it is the file on Mr. Djapic. The first three pages are translated. The next two pages merely are the numbers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would say the first three pages are originally in English. I do not see any translation into B/C/S, as a matter of fact. And then the following pages are not in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They are information that just identifies this individual as this KN 01432 B, to which is cross-referenced at the beginning, when the -- when the medical examiner did the autopsy, they operated not on identities but simple on numbers and the backup documents are in there from the OTP's file simply to support that view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although it seems that not much explanation has been given as to how the remains were identified as belonging to Mr. Djapic. It says, at least from what I can -- it's a long list where they give the numbers and then say, this is A, this is B, this is C, and on what basis is unclear. Finally, you have put to the witness that the autopsy report says that he -- I think you said he died before the mortar attack or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's a gunshot wound to the head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I have looked at -- it's a -- yes. Well, that is the -- that's part of what has been established and it is the conclusion of the one who had identify what among part of the head missing, a lot of bones of the head missing, all kind of other things that he concluded that this was the cause of death where it is further explained that the findings are not inconsistent with, for example, a head injury or shot. At least it is -- you summarized it very briefly by saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I did and, with all due respect to the Colonel not being a forensic examiner, I attempted to do that, Judge, simply because the expert comes to a particular conclusion that there were other wounds but that the cause of death was a wound -- a gunshot to the cranium or to the head that was antemortem, prior to his death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now there exactly I was a bit concerned that your lack of expertise -- isn't it true that antemortem or post-mortem or, as it says, three categories, antemortem, post-mortem ought not to be defined -- means whether the damage to the remains was caused after the death, post-mortem, or before the death which means that it could be the reason of the death so, Mr. Kehoe, your explanation of what antemortem and post-mortem in this context means might need some further study.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do not profess to be a forensic pathologist [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... nevertheless, you make statements on that and I was a bit afraid that putting to this witness that the cause -- that the cause of death was from before, I -- as a matter of fact, I could not exclude for the possibility that you misinterpreted where it says antemortem, because antemortem could well be cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Antemortem -- the way the context of these reports are written is whether or not these wounds to the cranium took place prior to death or after death. Now that comes from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or causing death.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, no. They're two different issues for a forensic pathologist. Off times you will see a forensic pathologist talk about a wound and based on the wound and lividity and a variety of other issues, they can make a determination whether or not this bruising or this wound was caused after the person was dead or before. Now this particular forensic pathologist, which is the one that the OTP hired, came to the conclusion that the cause of death, notwithstanding other injuries, was the gunshot to the head, which leads to the next step which I asked the Colonel. This individual, and certainly the one that was old, in all likelihood were dead prior to the mortar actually hitting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a couple of steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Of course. Of course, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not further discuss the matter. But, of course, I started by saying that we get an autopsy report. There's a whole file, part of it not translated, where of course the Chamber would like to always be informed. We had before the break that you said, Well, one picture, another one was attached. Here it is not just the autopsy report but it's more. It's a seven-page document partly not translated and it is presented to us -- and of course it is of less concern that it is presented to the witness because you focus his attention to only the portion shown to him but of course, for the Chamber, the whole of the document, everything is in evidence, and therefore, I would have appreciated if you would have said that you -- that you tendered the whole file related to the autopsy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will correct the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then it's three minutes to 7.00. I don't think, Mr. Kuzmanovic, that it makes any sense to start your cross-examination at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, three minutes won't do it, Your Honour. I do have probably less than half an hour, but I would not want to impose on anyone at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Williams, we'd like to see you back tomorrow. We start tomorrow at 9.00 in this same courtroom. I would like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony, either the testimony you have given already today, or the testimony you most likely will give tomorrow. Therefore, we adjourn and we resume tomorrow, 26th September, 9.00, Courtroom I.
